title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
blurb: Viktor Frankl was a Viennese psychiatrist who spent years as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps, including Auschwitz. In the first part of the book, he describes camp life from the inside. He traces how prisoners reacted in stages, from shock, to numbness, to the strange disorientation of liberation. He noticed that those who held on to a reason to live, such as a loved one, unfinished work, or a future goal, were often better able to endure. In the second part, Frankl explains logotherapy, his approach to psychology. He argues that our deepest drive is not pleasure or power but meaning. He says we can find it through what we create, through what and whom we love, and through the attitude we choose toward suffering we cannot avoid.

lessons.b: When Frankl lost his home, family, work and even his name in the camps, he discovered that a person's inner life cannot be fully taken away.

lessons.t: Shock, Numbness and the Mind's Defenses
lessons.b: Frankl observed that prisoners moved through stages of shock, apathy and disoriented release, and that the numbness was a way to protect the mind.

scene 7: The JOY bar is about 80% full. That contradicts the narration's 'feeling no joy at all' and the idea of slowly relearning how to feel. (fix: Show the bar nearly empty (about 10–15%), or animate it filling only slightly, so it reads as joy just beginning to return.)

scene 7: The person floats in mid-air above the flowers, well above the ground line, so they do not read as walking through the meadow. (fix: Lower the figure so it stands on the ground line among the flowers, with the flowers in front of or around it.)

lessons.b: Even when every outside freedom is gone, we keep the freedom to choose our attitude toward what happens to us.
